_sources.ipcc_sectors: IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2006gl/). Descriptions are verbatim quotes from the cited section of each volume. Per-entry citations are in the `source` field. NOTE: `sector_transport` is reported as 1A3 (sub of Energy) but tracked separately for policy purposes; `sector_agriculture` and `sector_lulucf` are presented separately to match legacy 1996 / CRT reporting (the 2006 Guidelines combine them as AFOLU, so descriptions for these two are extracted from AFOLU's enumerated components); `sector_other` is project-defined and is NOT an IPCC sector.
_sources.nbs_categories: Methodology development process for Git Hub.pdf, Table 2. Names and descriptions verbatim from the PDF. The PDF in turn cites IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land and Natural Climate Solutions (Griscom et al. 2017).
_sources.globe_categories: BIOFIN GLOBE 2024 taxonomy as curated by the team in dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx (sheet "Globe Taxonomy"). All descriptions are verbatim from column B. See per-entry `source` field.
_sources.globe_subcategories: BIOFIN GLOBE 2024 taxonomy authoritative XLSX at dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx. Descriptions are verbatim from column D ("Definitions / Examples") of each subcategory row. For codes where BIOFIN has no description (currently only 4.07), text is verbatim from the corresponding bullet in the SharePoint Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx — see per-entry `source` field. IDs match BIOFIN canonical numbering (no project renumbering).

ipcc_sectors.name: Energy
ipcc_sectors.description: The energy sector mainly comprises: exploration and exploitation of primary energy sources, conversion of primary energy sources into more useable energy forms in refineries and power plants, transmission and distribution of fuels, use of fuels in stationary and mobile applications. Emissions arise from these activities by combustion and as fugitive emissions, or escape without combustion.
ipcc_sectors.source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 2 Ch. 1 §1.2 (Source Categories) — verbatim

ipcc_sectors.name: Transport
ipcc_sectors.description: Mobile sources produce direct greenhouse gas emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) from the combustion of various fuel types. Greenhouse gas emissions from mobile combustion are most easily estimated by major transport activity, i.e., road, off-road, air, railways, and water-borne navigation. (1A3 TRANSPORT: Emissions from the combustion and evaporation of fuel for all transport activity, excluding military transport, regardless of the sector, specified by sub-categories below.) Reported as IPCC code 1A3, a sub-category of Energy, but tracked separately here for policy purposes.
ipcc_sectors.source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 2 Ch. 3 §3.1 (Overview) + Table 3.1.1 (1A3 Transport) — verbatim quotes; framing sentence about policy-purpose split is project-added

ipcc_sectors.name: Industrial processes and product use
ipcc_sectors.description: This volume, Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU), covers greenhouse gas emissions occurring from industrial processes, from the use of greenhouse gases in products, and from non-energy uses of fossil fuel carbon. The main emission sources are releases from industrial processes that chemically or physically transform materials (for example, the blast furnace in the iron and steel industry, ammonia and other chemical products manufactured from fossil fuels used as chemical feedstock and the cement industry are notable examples of industrial processes that release a significant amount of CO2). During these processes, many different greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and perfluorocarbons (PFCs), can be produced.
ipcc_sectors.source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 3 Ch. 1 §1.1 (Introduction) — verbatim, paragraphs 1-2

ipcc_sectors.name: Agriculture
ipcc_sectors.description: Sub-sector of AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use) covering, per the AFOLU Sector Guidance and methods enumeration: CH4 emission from livestock (enteric fermentation); CH4 and N2O emissions from manure management systems; CH4 emissions from rice cultivation; N2O emissions from all managed soils; CO2 emissions associated with liming and urea application to managed soils.
ipcc_sectors.source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 4 Ch. 1 §1.1 — verbatim items from the AFOLU 'Guidance and methods' enumeration; framing as a separate Agriculture sub-sector matches legacy 1996 / CRT reporting (2006 Guidelines treat AFOLU as one sector)

ipcc_sectors.name: Land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF)
ipcc_sectors.description: Sub-sector of AFOLU covering, per the 2006 Guidelines: CO2 emissions and removals resulting from C stock changes in biomass, dead organic matter and mineral soils, for all managed lands; CO2 and non-CO2 emissions from fire on all managed land; CO2 and N2O emissions from cultivated organic soils; CO2 and N2O emissions from managed wetlands; C stock change associated with harvested wood products. Six land-use categories used in GPG-LULUCF (i.e., Forest Land, Cropland, Grassland, Wetlands, Settlements, and Other Land), further sub-divided into land remaining in the same category and land converted from one category to another.
ipcc_sectors.source: IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Vol. 4 Ch. 1 §1.1 — verbatim items from the AFOLU 'Guidance and methods' enumeration plus the six-land-use-categories paragraph; framing as a separate LULUCF sub-sector matches legacy 1996 / CRT reporting

ipcc_sectors.name: Waste
ipcc_sectors.description: The Waste volume gives methodological guidance for estimation of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from following categories: Solid waste disposal (Chapter 3); Biological treatment of solid waste (Chapter 4); Incineration and open burning of waste (Chapter 5); Wastewater treatment and discharge (Chapter 6).

ipcc_sectors.name: Other / Cross-cutting
ipcc_sectors.description: Project-defined catch-all (NOT an IPCC sector) for policy measures that span multiple IPCC sectors or do not fit any single sector. Used for cross-cutting frameworks, institutional capacity, education, gender mainstreaming, finance mechanisms, and health- or water-related climate measures.
ipcc_sectors.source: Project-defined; not present in IPCC 2006 Guidelines

nbs_categories.description: This includes coastal zone risk retention, living shorelines, tidal basins, oyster beds, artificial reefs, tidal salt marshes, sustainable coastal management, marine production promotion, coastal environment monitoring and risk assessment, disease management of marine resources, mangrove protection, coral reef protection, seagrass protection, marine protected areas, restoring marine ecosystems, coastal wetland, seagrass, coral reef and mangrove restoration, sustainable fishery, marine ecosystem service management, tidal salt marshes, restoration of seagrass beds, mangroves, terrestrial.

nbs_categories.name: Agriculture and livestock management
nbs_categories.description: This includes terrestrial ecosystems, climate-resilient crops, climate-resilient livestock management, climate-smart agriculture, parametric insurance, regenerative agriculture, agroecology, crop diversification, community-seeds banks, integrated water management, grazing land management, manure management, agricultural land and soil management, agriculture and livestock disease management, sustainable agricultural education and consulting, agroforestry, agricultural diversification, improved grazing land management, reduced grassland conversion to cropland, sustainable rangeland management, sustainable land management, sustainable grazing, optimal grazing intensity, conservation agriculture, landscape restoration, nature-positive dietary changes, reducing food waste, reducing post-harvest losses, sustainable sourcing and use of resources, supply-chain diversification, improved food processing and retailing, improved energy use in food systems, reducing food loss, and improved supply chain resilience.

nbs_categories.name: Water management
nbs_categories.description: This includes catchment protection, sustainable irrigation, watershed restoration, freshwater ecosystem restoration, integrated water resource management, water management systems, securing water quality, water education and consulting, monitoring of water resources, service management of water ecosystems, and pluvial flood risk reduction.

nbs_categories.name: Forest management, restoration, and protection
nbs_categories.description: This includes natural forest management, improved plantations, sustainable forestry practices, preventing illegal logging, reducing deforestation and forest degradation, fire management, REDD+, reforestation, afforestation, tree planting on degraded land, temperate and tropical forest restoration, forest carbon sink management, and monitoring forest changes.

nbs_categories.name: Protection and restoration of wetlands and freshwater ecosystems
nbs_categories.description: This includes river, inland water and wetland protection, peatland rewetting, avoiding peat impacts, freshwater ecosystem protection, wetland management, service management of freshwater ecosystems, peatland restoration, dune restoration, freshwater ecosystem restoration, catchment restoration, watershed protection, restoration and reduced conversion of coastal wetlands, restoration and reduced conversion of peatlands, sustainable fishery, and restoring peatlands.

nbs_categories.name: Ecosystem protection and connectivity
nbs_categories.description: This includes establishing protected areas, community reserves, wildlife corridors, restore pollinator habitats, prevent species extinction, habitat rewilding, restricting invasive species and pests, ecosystem change detection, other effective conservation measures (OECM), and increased connectivity between protected areas.

nbs_categories.name: Soil fertility management and restoration
nbs_categories.description: This includes increased soil organic carbon, reduced soil erosion, reduced soil salinization, reduced soil compaction, conservation tillage, biochar application, improved cropland soil management, soil restoration, soil improvement, and sustainable intensification.

nbs_categories.name: Nature-based risk management and disaster prevention
nbs_categories.description: This includes agricultural disaster management and invasive alien species and pest control, disease surveillance, wildfire management, fire management, flood control, infrastructure and critical systems resilience, reduced landslides and hazards, making human settlement safer, environmental risk monitoring, forecasting and warning systems, resource-based early warnings, reduced pollution, acidification prevention, disaster risk reduction and management in agriculture, security and diversification in critical sectors such as energy, food and water, risk sharing instruments and insurance, livelihood diversification, and management of urban sprawl (blue and green spaces).

nbs_categories.name: Nature-based carbon sequestration
nbs_categories.description: This includes Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS), enhanced weathering of minerals, tree planting for carbon sequestration, afforestation, reforestation, proforestation, tree intercropping, silvopasture, restore forests for carbon sequestration, and improved plantations for carbon storage.

nbs_categories.name: Urban settlements management
nbs_categories.description: This includes urban green spaces, sponge city, urban forests, green roofs, green walls, urban wetlands, rain gardens, vegetated stormwater systems, green infrastructure, urban farms.

globe_categories.name: Access and benefit sharing
globe_categories.description:
Access to genetic resources, with a focus on prior informed consent, and the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits of genetic diversity with those whose knowledge is used, on Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) and taking into account all rights over those resources, and by appropriate funding.

Actions can include: 
- Bioprospecting/ Screening for biodiversity areas and establishing permitting processes: Regulating the screening for biodiversity areas and resources for commercial use and all processes that allow this research. 
- Contractual arrangements: Arrangements between genetic resource (knowledge) provider and user, the provider and the state as well as the user and the state that ensure legal certainty and transparency about access to genetic resources, the involvement of the local population, allow for research, as well as how the financial and non-financial benefit of the use is shared. The compliance of the arrangements needs to be supported.
- Benefit-sharing mechanism: The commitment to channel a fair share of the benefits for the use of genetic resources, whether monetary or non-monetary, back to the range of designated participants. Benefit-sharing mechanisms can be monetary or non-monetary 
- Nagoya Protocol: It focuses on the institutional structures of the protocol, and expenditures related explicitly to the ratification and Nagoya-specific processes (e.g. designation of a national focal point, ABS clearing house mechanism), in addition to capacity-building and awareness raising.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 2 column B

globe_categories.name: Biodiversity awareness and knowledge
globe_categories.description:
Biodiversity awareness and knowledge includes a wide range of different topics. Biodiversity knowledge aims to produce, generate and provide an easy and timely access to quality data and information, to support all efforts in halting biodiversity loss or maintaining and increasing current biodiversity levels. Knowledge generation and distribution  includes formal and non-formal contexts, technical training, biodiversity communication and scientific research, the indigenous and local communities' knowledge.

Actions can include: 
- Formal education: Integration of biodiversity into hierarchically structured, chronologically graded educational system running from primary through the tertiary institutions.
- Non-formal and informal biodiversity education: planned, structured programmes and processes outside the formal educational curriculum, designed to improve a range of skills and competencies related to biodiversity and the KMGBF and shift individual acquires attitudes and values. 
- Biodiversity awareness and communication: Efforts to bring public awareness to issues relating to biodiversity to the attention of key groups who have the power to influence outcomes. Can include campaigns, surveys, events, and establishment of physical spaces, such as parks or zoos, to enable people to encounter biodiversity in their daily lives. 
- Biodiversity scientific research: Includes assessments and studies undertaken on a systematic basis in order to increase the stock of knowledge on biodiversity,  methods to collect, process, and exchange biodiversity data. Can be citizen science and community and indigenous-lead knowledge creation. 
Indigenous and local communities knowledge - Promotion, protection, and utilization of knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities for biodiversity decision-making, with FPIC. Traditional knowledge tends to be collectively owned and takes the form of stories, songs, folklore, proverbs, cultural values, beliefs, rituals, local language, and agricultural practices, including the development of plant species and animal breeds.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 3 column B

globe_categories.name: Biosafety
globe_categories.description:
Includes two sub-categories: 
(1) Prevention, containment, and eradication of invasive alien species (IAS) Invasive alien species (IAS) and (2) safe handling, transport and use of living modified organisms (LMOs/GMOs) resulting from modern biotechnology that may have adverse effects on biological diversity. 

Actions include: 
- Identification and prioritization of IAS species, their introduction pathways and most effective measures to avoid direct or indirect introduction and their impacts: Defintiion. 
-Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs), including Living modified organisms (LMO): DEFINITTION. Includes standards and regulation to ensure the precautionary principle before introducing modified species, research,  biosafety evaluation, and capacity building on impacts of GMOs, and Compliance to international and regional and sub-regional agreements on Biosafety, in particular the Cartagena Protocol.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 4 column B

globe_categories.name: Green economy
globe_categories.description:
A green economy results in improved human well-being and social equity, while significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities and can be considered as one that is low in carbon, resource efficient, and socially inclusive. 

Actions include: 

- Green supply chain: Establishing a green supply chain that integrates environmentally responsible practices related to sourcing, product design, manufacturing, packaging, logistics and end-of-life product management, improving efficiency, reducing emissions, used resources and waste. 
- Reduction of harm to biodiversity in extractive industries: Can include disclosure of environmental impact by extractive activities and mitigation measures taken
- Sustainable consumption: Reduction of negative impact on biodiversity by improving the ecological footprint, reducing per-capita consumption, avoiding waste and overexploitation.
- Sustainable energy: Reduction of negative impacts of energy production, transmission and distribution, Innovative energy systems  not harming (or even supporting) biodiversity conservation, disclosure of environmental impacts in energy production. 
- Sustainable tourism: Tourism that takes full account of its current and future economic, social and environmental impacts, addressing the needs of visitors, the industry, the environment and host communities. 
- Sustainable transportation: Aiming for reducing the negative impacts by reducing the reliance on natural resources, providing environmentally friendly alternatives (e.g. bike, pedestrian) and increasing public transport
- Sustainable urban and rural areas: Can include environmental impact assessments of infrastructure projects, improving water quality, and disaster risk reduction.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 5 column B

globe_categories.name: Biodiversity planning and finance
globe_categories.description:
National, state or local planning, policy, finance, legal, coordination and enforcement actions crosscutting in nature that cover multiple biodiversity categories or general issues, such as biodiversity planning and policy. 

Activities include: 
- Biodiversity laws, policies, and plans: Change, creation and implementation of biodiversity laws, policies, and plans, harmonization of standards and disclosure by companies and public projects, measures to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services by financial institutions, business, public institutions and other relevant actors, including the civil society, and prosecution and judgement of any infringement of biodiversity-relevant law, as well as national and international biodiversity-relevant crimes. 
Policy coherence: policy coherence and mainstreaming to include biodiversity relevant aspects in all other sector's plans, policies, regulations and decision-making processes. 
- Biodiversity coordination and management: Includes the update of NBSAPs including all stakeholders, including indigenous peoples, local communities, and women, science-based monitoring and evaluation for adaptive management, support for community-based approaches and conservation, ensuring free, prior, and informed consent, and protection for environmental defenders. 
- Biodiversity finance planning and coordination: Measures to increase domestic and international finance flows to biodiversity, by introducing new instruments and mechanisms, improving the spending of currently available funds and by providing legal frameworks for non-public actors.
- Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) Framework: Undertaking formal, systematic process to analyse and address the environmental effects of policies, plans and programmes and other strategic initiatives. 
- Spatial planning: Developing spatial data and spatial arrangements of all kinds of territories to use it in a rational way, coordinating the different interests (production, livelihood, biodiversity conservation, historical/cultural value, recreation…) and sectorial policies.  
Multi-lateral environmental agreements: Ratification, implementation and monitoring of relevant conventions focusing directly on biodiversity: Convention on Biological Diversity and its protocols, Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals, The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA), Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar Convention), World Heritage Convention (WHC), High Seas Treaty, International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC), including regional conventions and those related to environmental rights (e.g. Aarhus Convention, Escazu Agreement). This also can include all other conventions, initiatives and alliances  that either tackle biodiversity loss drivers or broader environmental objectives, e.g. UNCLOS, any Pollution-related Convention, UNFCCC, etc
- Access to resources, information and decision-making, including FPIC consultations: Directed financial and non-financial resources to all kind of rights holders and stakeholders, in particular to Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth, as well as having access to complete and accurate information and being involved as key-partners or main actor in decision-making processes, including the right to free, prior, informed consent (FPIC).
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 6 column B

globe_categories.name: Pollution management
globe_categories.description:
Pollution is the introduction of harmful materials (i.e. pollutants) into the environment at a faster rate than can be dispersed, diluted, decomposed, recycled, or stored in some harmless form. It can be natural (e.g. Vulcan ashes) or human-made and in any form (solid, liquid, or gas, but also energy). Biodiversity benefits from its  management, consisting of pollution prevention at the source, reduction, reusing, recycling, treatment or disposal. 

Activities can include: 
-Protection and remediation of soil, groundwater and surface water: Measures and activities aimed at the prevention of pollutant infiltration, cleaning up of soils and water bodies and the protection of soil from erosion and other physical degradation as well as from salinisation. Monitoring, control of soil and groundwater pollution is included.
-Protection of ambient air and climate: Activities aimed at the reduction of emissions into the ambient air or ambient concentrations of air pollutants as well as to measures and activities aimed at the control of emissions of greenhouse gases and gases that adversely affect the stratospheric ozone layer. Note: Ensure that the biodiversity intention is clearly stated - only CO2 reduction is not sufficient as biodiversity purpose
-Waste management: Reduced/Avoided pollution by managing all kinds of waste, including wastewater. 
-Coastal and marine pollution debris management: Reduced/Avoided coastal and marine pollution debris with activities tackling land- and sea-based sources, focusing especially on plastic
-Other pollution management measures: Other pollutant includes: noise, vibration, light, temperature, radiation, and, partially pharmaceutical, heavy metals, Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB)
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 7 column B

globe_categories.name: Protected areas and other conservation measures
globe_categories.description:
In situ and ex situ measures to protect and safeguard biodiversity at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. The effort can be area-based through protected areas, their expansion, connection or buffer zones; but also includes other conservation measures, e.g. focusing on specific species (in particular migratory species) or establishing other effective conservation measures.

Activities can include: 
- Management and expansion of Protected Areas, including Indigenous and Communities Conserved Areas (ICCA):  Maintaining or establishing protected areas which are designated or regulated and managed to achieve specific conservation objectives. It includes all IUCN Categories (Ia-VI), as well as defined Indigenous and Community Conserved Areas (ICCA). The expansion of Protected Areas includes the analysis of potential areas, identifying the best management policy considering the local circumstances (ecological and social), securing land titles and legal designation of the area.
- Management of areas outside of Protected Areas: All activities undertaken to manage, protect and develop areas outside of the Protected Area regime such as transboundary areas, biodiversity corridors, Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), landscapes and seascapes to achieve the long-term conservation of nature with associated ecosystem services and cultural values. It includes all action of public institution and ministries, as well as providing the framework and support for individuals, communities, non-public institutions and businesses, to maintain, enhance, and restore ecological flows, species movement, and dynamic processes across intact and fragmented environments outside of PA.
- Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM): Governance and management of areas outside of Protected Areas in ways that achieve positive and sustained long-term outcomes for the in situ conservation of biodiversity, with associated ecosystem functions and services and where applicable, cultural, spiritual, socio–economic, and other locally relevant values. The main difference between a protected area and an OECM is that PAs have a primary conservation objective, however it even remained declared as such when becoming ineffective, whereas an OECM delivers the effective in-situ conservation of biodiversity, regardless of its objectives.
- Conservation of species - Related to the targeted protection of species, in particular wildlife and migratory species, within or outside of protected and conserved areas. That includes reducing threats such as overconsumption, trade and poaching; climate change; displacement; reduced habitats; Invasive Alien Species, but also conservation measures in- and ex-situ.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 8 column B

globe_categories.name: Restoration
globe_categories.description:
Ecosystem restoration means assisting in the recovery of ecosystems that have been degraded or destroyed, as well as conserving the ecosystems that are still intact. It should result in a rehabilitation of the ecosystem functions and services. Restoration efforts are recognized to support the achievement of all Rio Conventions – Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), as well as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Activities can include: 
- Reintroduction and translocation of species: Capture, transport and release or introduction of species, habitats or other ecological material (such as soil) from one location to another to support habitat or species restoration. 
- Site redevelopment and engineering: Efforts to prevent ecosysten degradation and repair damage already caused, for example by removing drivers of degradation, clean up after chemical or physical damage, and resotration of river channels. 
- Site management - Ongoing management or maintenance of restoration sites after the restoration activity has been realized to ensure the continuity of the initiated trajectory or status quo. This could include setting managment planning, awareness raising on restoration,  and lanscape care and maintenance.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 9 column B

globe_categories.name: Sustainable use
globe_categories.description:
Sustainable Use is the use of components of biological diversity in a way and at a rate that does not lead to the long-term decline of biological diversity, thereby maintaining its potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations. This category is distinguished from the green economy by its focus on ecosystem services, primarily production and the underlying support services. Activities are targeted towards improving biodiversity outcomes in coordination with other co-benefits related to natural resource use.

Activities include: 
- Agrobiodiversity: Agricultural biodiversity, is also known as agrobiodiversity or the genetic resources for food and agriculture.  Inventory, surveys and statistics of genetic variety for food and other consumption can support agrobiodiversity, as well as on-farm consesrvation of species, development and maintence of seed banks, incentives and regulation to encourage the sustainable plantation/farming of local, traditional or conservation varieties of species, guidelines and policies that protect wild relatives of domestically used species, and implementation of the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA).
- Sustainable Agriculture (crops and livestock): Sustainable agriculture seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood) in the food production system. It can comprise a wide range of practices based on traditional and local knowledge or use innovative approaches including robots or Artificial Intelligence; from urban to rural farming as well as production other than food (e.g., fibre, biofuel).
- Sustainable aquaculture:  The controlled cultivation or farming of fish, shellfish, and aquatic plants. The purpose is to create a source of aquatic-sourced food and commercial products in a way that will increase availability while reducing environmental harm and protecting various aquatic species. includes mariculture, but excludes open-pens. 
- Sustainable fisheries: The shift to sustainable fisheries (both lethal and non-lethal) includes measures to combat overfishing, ensuring habitat protection, and use of non-aggressive fishing devices. 
- Sustainable forestry: Sustainable forestry seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood). That means considering the needs of wildlife and its forest ecosystem with its abiotic components such as soil and water. Sustainable forestry therefore includes all kind of human intervention in forests that safeguard biodiversity.
- Sustainable freshwater: Measures that reduces the overuse of freshwater resources (e.g. for drink water supply or agriculture), or other threats to the freshwater ecosystem as pollution (e.g. by industry or agriculture sector and habitated areas), climate change, invasive alien species and obstacles (especially dams), as well as tools that allow for better reporting and monitoring*. Indigenous people and local communities living close by the freshwater or traditionally using it should be included and considered when measurements are planned and implemented.
- Sustainable marine and coastal management: Sustainable marine and coastal management seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood).
- Sustainable rangelands: Sustainable rangeland management seeks to combine environmental protection (for wildlife, different habitats and watersheds), production and related income (especially by livestock, freshwater) as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood). That means considering the needs of wildlife and its related ecosystem (e.g. grassland, shrubland, wetland) with its abiotic components such as soil and water. Sustainable rangelands therefore include all kind of human intervention in rangelands that safeguard biodiversity, such as avoiding erosion and reduced risk of fire, while benefitting from the rangeland products and services within the ecological limits, while including Indigenous Peoples and local communities equitably.
- Sustainable wildlife: Wildlife refers to captive or living in the wild organisms that have not been subject to breeding. All uses of wildlife, such as fishing, gathering, logging and terrestrial animal harvesting should be done within the ecological limits.
globe_categories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 10 column B

globe_subcategories.name: Non-formal and informal biodiversity education
globe_subcategories.description:
Non-formal education — planned, structured programmes and processes of personal and social education outside the formal educational curriculum, designed to improve a range of skills and competencies. 
Informal education is the process whereby every individual acquires attitudes, values, skills and knowledge from daily experience, such as family, friends, peers and media.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "2 Awareness - Knowledge" row 16 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Biodiversity awareness and communication
globe_subcategories.description:
Awareness - Public awareness brings the issues relating to biodiversity to the attention of key groups who have the power to influence outcomes. Awareness is an agenda setting and marketing exercise helping people to know what and why this is an important issue, the aspirations for the targets, and what is and can be done to achieve these. 
Communication - Trying to bring the meaning of biodiversity (causes of loss, solutions, conservation needs, biodiversity finance, governance, etc) to different audiences and target groups, by providing information by all kinds of means. In an instrumental approach government use communication with other instruments to support biodiversity conservation to address economic constraints and to motivate action. Governments also use one-way communication to inform audiences about policies and legislation.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "2 Awareness - Knowledge" row 30 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Biodiversity Scientific research
globe_subcategories.description: Research comprises creative work undertaken on a systematic basis in order to increase the stock of knowledge and the use of this knowledge.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "2 Awareness - Knowledge" row 42 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Indigenous and local communities* knowledge*
globe_subcategories.description: Knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities around the world. Developed from experience gained over the centuries and adapted to the local culture and environment, traditional knowledge is transmitted orally from generation to generation. It tends to be collectively owned and takes the form of stories, songs, folklore, proverbs, cultural values, beliefs, rituals, community laws, local language, and agricultural practices, including the development of plant species and animal breeds. Traditional knowledge is mainly of a practical nature, particularly in such fields as agriculture, fisheries, health, horticulture, and forestry.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "2 Awareness - Knowledge" row 64 column D

globe_subcategories.name: CBD clearing-house mechanism
globe_subcategories.description: Its mission is to contribute significantly to the implementation of the Convention on Biological Diversity and its Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020, through effective information services and other appropriate means in order to promote and facilitate scientific and technical cooperation, knowledge sharing and information exchange, and to establish a fully operational network of Parties and partners.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "2 Awareness - Knowledge" row 74 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Invasive Alien Species
globe_subcategories.description:
for collection of data; 2 BD Awareness and Knowledge might be relevant; including citizen-sciences
for long-term measures: most measures are part of 8 Restoration
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "3 Biosafety" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs), including Living modified organisms (LMO)
globe_subcategories.description: GMO/LMO have many potential benefits, however, also might cause harm. Thus, one of the main points is research, collaboration and establishing relevant policies and regulation that allow advancing the research, without putting biodiversity into danger. It also requires trainings, capacity-building*, awareness raising, and the monitoring of the procedures put in place to handle GMO/LMO
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "3 Biosafety" row 16 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Green supply chain
globe_subcategories.description: A green supply chain integrates environmentally responsible practices related to sourcing, product design, manufacturing, packaging, logistics and end-of-life product management, improving efficiency, reducing emissions, used resources and waste*.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Extractive industries
globe_subcategories.description:
Note: Ensure that the biodiversity intention is clearly stated
For some countries, the recovery of raw materials (extractive sector) is critical for domestic resource mobilization and prof-its could be channelled to biodiversity-friendly investments. Countries should ensure that impact on biodiversity is avoided or minimized as much as possible.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 12 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable consumption
globe_subcategories.description: The aim is to reduce the negative impact on biodiversity by improving the ecological footprint, reducing per-capita consumption, avoiding waste and overexploitation.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 21 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable energy
globe_subcategories.description: Note: Ensure that the biodiversity intention is clearly stated
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 31 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable tourism
globe_subcategories.description: Tourism that takes full account of its current and future economic, social and environmental impacts, addressing the needs of visitors, the industry, the environment and host communities
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 37 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable transportation
globe_subcategories.description: aiming for reducing the negative impacts by reducing the reliance on natural resources, providing environmentally friendly alternatives (e.g. bike, pedestrian) and increasing public transport
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "4 Green Economy" row 47 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable urban and rural areas
globe_subcategories.description: Can include environmental impact assessments of infrastructure projects, improving water quality, and disaster risk reduction.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/sharepoint_sync/Insight I taxonomy/Globe Taxonomy categories.xlsx, sheet "Globe Taxonomy" row 5 column B (bullet for "Sustainable urban and rural areas"). BIOFIN authoritative XLSX has no definition cell for this code.

globe_subcategories.name: Biodiversity laws, policies, plans
globe_subcategories.description: All legal work on every level of government (national, state or local) that has the main objective to address Biodiversity directly
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Other relevant laws, policies, plans
globe_subcategories.description: Again all kinds of legal work on every level of government, however only addressing biodiversity indirectly (e.g. legislation related to non-biodiversity sectors)
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 9 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Biodiversity coordination and management
globe_subcategories.description: The coordination with different stake-* and rightsholders*, on a local, national or international level, either with the state participating or providing a framework/ platform for other actors to coordinate among themselves.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 14 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Biodiversity finance planning and coordination
globe_subcategories.description: All kind of measures that can increase domestic and international finance flows, by introducing new instruments and mechanisms, improving the spending of currently available funds and by providing legal frameworks for non-public actors.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 24 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)* Framework
globe_subcategories.description: formal, systematic process to analyse and address the environmental effects of policies, plans and programmes and other strategic initiatives, usually done in their early stages
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 39 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Spatial planning
globe_subcategories.description: Relates to the spatial arrangement of all kinds of territories to use it in a rational way, coordinating the different interests (production, livelihood, biodiversity conservation, historical/cultural value, recreation…) and sectorial policies.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 43 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Multilateral environmental agreements
globe_subcategories.description: Note: Implementation of concrete actions to comply with those agreements are in the specific subcategories
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 51 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Access to resources, information and decision-making, including FPIC* consultations
globe_subcategories.description: Directed financial and non-financial resources to all kind of rights holders* and stakeholders*, in particular to Indigenous Peoples and local communities*, women and youth, as well as having access to complete and accurate information and being involved as key-partners or main actor in decision-making processes, including the right to free, prior, informed consent (FPIC).
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "5 Planning and Finance" row 56 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Protection and remediation of soil, groundwater and surface water
globe_subcategories.description: Measures and activities aimed at the prevention of pollutant infiltration, cleaning up of soils and water bodies and the protection of soil from erosion and other physical degradation as well as from salinisation. Monitoring*, control of soil and groundwater pollution is included.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Protection of ambient air and climate
globe_subcategories.description:
Activities aimed at the reduction of emissions into the ambient air or ambient concentrations of air pollutants as well as to measures and activities aimed at the control of emissions of greenhouse gases and gases that adversely affect the stratospheric ozone layer.
Note: Ensure that the biodiversity intention is clearly stated - only CO2 reduction is not sufficient as biodiversity purpose
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 14 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Waste* management
globe_subcategories.description:
Reduced/Avoided pollution by managing all kinds of waste, including wastewater*
Note: Ensure that the biodiversity intention is clearly stated
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 28 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Coastal and marine pollution debris* management
globe_subcategories.description:
Reduced/Avoided coastal and marine pollution debris with activities tackling land- and sea-based sources, focusing especially on plastic
Note: If there are direct links to a production system of Sustainable Use, expenditure should be counted there.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 41 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Other pollution management measures
globe_subcategories.description: other pollutant includes: noise, vibration, light, temperature, radiation, and, partially pharmaceutical, heavy metals, Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)*, Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB)
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 52 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Enabling activities related to all types of pollution
globe_subcategories.description: general activities related to awareness raising, capacity building and data generation for all type of pollution, in case those activities have clear biodiversity objectives
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "6 Pollution Management" row 62 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Management and expansion of PAs, including Indigenous and Communities Conserved Areas (ICCA)*
globe_subcategories.description: A protected area is a geographically defined area which is designated or regulated and managed to achieve specific conservation objectives. It includes all IUCN Categories (Ia-VI), as well as defined Indigenous and Community Conserved Areas (ICCA). The expansion of Protected Areas includes the analysis of potential areas, identifying the best management policy considering the local circumstances (ecological and social), securing land titles and legal designation of the area.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "7 PA & other measures" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Management of areas outside of PAs
globe_subcategories.description:
All activities undertaken to manage, protect and develop areas outside of the Protected Area regime such as transboundary areas, biodiversity corridors, Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), landscapes and seascapes to achieve the long-term conservation of nature with associated ecosystem services and cultural values. It includes all action of public institution and ministries, as well as providing the framework and support for individuals, communities, non-public institutions and businesses, to maintain, enhance, and restore ecological flows, species movement, and dynamic processes across intact and fragmented environments outside of PA.
Note: In case an area is an designated OECM area, refer to subcategory 7.03 OECM
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "7 PA & other measures" row 29 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM)
globe_subcategories.description: A geographically defined area other than a Protected Area, which is governed and managed in ways that achieve positive and sustained long-term outcomes for the in situ conservation of biodiversity, with associated ecosystem functions and services and where applicable, cultural, spiritual, socio–economic, and other locally relevant values (CBD, 2018). The main difference between a protected area and an OECM is that PAs have a primary conservation objective, however it even remained declared as such when becoming ineffective, whereas an OECM delivers the effective in-situ conservation of biodiversity, regardless of its objectives.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "7 PA & other measures" row 41 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Conservation of species
globe_subcategories.description: Related to the targeted protection of species, in particular wildlife and migratory species, within or outside of protected and conserved areas. That includes reducing threats such as overconsumption, trade and poaching; climate change; displacement; reduced habitats; Invasive Alien Species, but also conservation measures in- and ex-situ.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "7 PA & other measures" row 48 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Reintroduction and translocation of species
globe_subcategories.description: Reintroduction generally refers to the introduction into the wild of species from captive stock, whereas translocation is the capture, transport and release or introduction of species, habitats or other ecological material (such as soil) from one location to another.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "8 Restoration" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Site redevelopment and engineering
globe_subcategories.description: Efforts should be both directed at preventing degradation in the first place, but also to repair damage already caused.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "8 Restoration" row 15 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Site management
globe_subcategories.description: Ongoing management or maintenance of restoration sites after the restoration activity has been realized to ensure the continuity of the initiated trajectory or status quo.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "8 Restoration" row 29 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Agrobiodiversity
globe_subcategories.description: Agricultural biodiversity, also known as agrobiodiversity or the genetic resources for food and agriculture. Agrobiodiversity is the result of natural selection processes and the careful selection and inventive developments of farmers, herders and fishers over millennia. Many people’s food and livelihood security depend on the sustained management of various biological resources that are important for food and agriculture.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 4 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable Agriculture (crops and livestock)
globe_subcategories.description: Sustainable agriculture seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood) in the food production system. It can comprise a wide range of practices based on traditional and local knowledge* or use innovative approaches including robots or Artificial Intelligence; from urban to rural farming as well as production other than food (e.g., fibre, biofuel).
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 15 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable Aquaculture
globe_subcategories.description:
The controlled cultivation or farming of fish, shellfish, and aquatic plants. The purpose is to create a source of aquatic-sourced food and commercial products in a way that will increase availability while reducing environmental harm and protecting various aquatic species.
includes mariculture, but excludes open-pens
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 35 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable Fisheries
globe_subcategories.description: The shift to sustainable fisheries (both lethal and non-lethal) includes measures to combat overfishing, ensuring habitat protection, and use of non-aggressive fishing devices, to name a few.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 47 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable Forestry
globe_subcategories.description: Sustainable forestry seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood). That means considering the needs of wildlife and its forest ecosystem with its abiotic components such as soil and water. Sustainable forestry therefore includes all kind of human intervention in forests that safeguard biodiversity.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 64 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable Freshwater
globe_subcategories.description: Measures that reduces the overuse of freshwater resources (e.g. for drink water supply or agriculture), or other threats to the freshwater ecosystem as pollution (e.g. by industry or agriculture sector and habitated areas), climate change, invasive alien species and obstacles (especially dams), as well as tools that allow for better reporting and monitoring*. Indigenous people and local communities living close by the freshwater or traditionally using it should be included and considered when measurements are planned and implemented.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 75 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable marine and coastal management
globe_subcategories.description: Sustainable marine and coastal management seeks to combine environmental protection, production and related income as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood).
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 85 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable rangelands
globe_subcategories.description: Sustainable rangeland management seeks to combine environmental protection (for wildlife, different habitats and watersheds), production and related income (especially by livestock, freshwater) as well as social equity (i.e. increased livelihood). That means considering the needs of wildlife and its related ecosystem (e.g. grassland, shrubland, wetland) with its abiotic components such as soil and water. Sustainable rangelands therefore include all kind of human intervention in rangelands that safeguard biodiversity, such as avoiding erosion and reduced risk of fire, while benefitting from the rangeland products and services within the ecological limits, while including Indigenous Peoples and local communities* equitably.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 95 column D

globe_subcategories.name: Sustainable wildlife
globe_subcategories.description:
Sustainable management of wildlife.
Wildlife refers to captive or living in the wild organisms that have not been subject to breeding. All uses - extractive* (fishing, gathering, logging and terrestrial animal harvesting) and non-extractive* - should be done within the ecological limits.
globe_subcategories.source: dev_data_scripts/biofin/2-8_taxonomy_globe.xlsx, sheet "9 Sustainable Use" row 104 column D
